title: WHY DID FIRE COME OUT OF A ROCK WHEN GIDEON OFFERED GOD A MEAL? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT THE FIRE THAT CONSUMED HIS OFFERING BUT SPARED HIS LIFE
paragraphs: WHY DID FIRE COME OUT OF A ROCK WHEN GIDEON OFFERED GOD A MEAL? THE TERRIFYING TRUTH ABOUT THE FIRE THAT CONSUMED HIS OFFERING BUT SPARED HIS LIFE

He thought he was preparing food for a stranger. He never imagined that one touch of a staff would unleash fire from a rock, consume everything he brought, and leave him trembling before the holiness of God. But the greatest miracle wasn't the fire. It was what God said to the frightened man who thought he was about to die.
There are moments when God interrupts your life so unexpectedly that everything you thought you knew about yourself begins to fall apart.
Sometimes, that interruption doesn't happen inside a church.
It doesn't happen while you're singing worship songs.
It doesn't even happen when you feel particularly close to God.
Sometimes, it happens when you're hiding.
When you're exhausted.
When you're simply trying to survive another day without falling apart.
And sometimes, the very place where you've been hiding your fear becomes the place where God reveals His glory.
That is where Gideon's story begins.
Not on a battlefield.
Not in a palace.
Not surrounded by thousands of soldiers cheering his name.
He was hiding in a winepress, threshing wheat.

And before his encounter was over, fire would rise from a rock, his offering would disappear, and a terrified man would discover something about the God of Israel that every wounded, ashamed, struggling believer desperately needs to understand.
The God whose holiness exposes us is also the God who graciously calls us to Himself.
But to understand why that fire appeared, we need to understand what was happening before Gideon ever prepared the meal.
Israel was suffering.
For seven years, the Midianites had oppressed God's people. Whenever the Israelites planted crops, their enemies would invade, destroy their produce, and devastate the land.
Imagine working for months, planting seeds, enduring the heat, waiting for harvest, only to watch someone else take everything.
Again.
And again.
And again.
Eventually, survival changes how a person thinks.
You stop dreaming about tomorrow because you're too busy trying to make it through today.
You stop expecting victory because disappointment has become familiar.
You learn to hide whatever little you have left.
That was Gideon's world.
And perhaps, in a different way, it has been yours.
You still believe in God, but life has been brutal.
You still pray, but some prayers seem unanswered.
You still read Scripture, but there are nights when fear speaks louder than the promises you remember.
People see you functioning.
They don't see the battle happening inside you.
They don't know how many times you've whispered, "Lord, how much longer?"
Gideon knew something about that kind of exhaustion.
And the Bible doesn't introduce him as a fearless champion.
Judges 6:11 describes him threshing wheat in a winepress to hide it from the Midianites.
A winepress was normally used for pressing grapes. Wheat was usually threshed in a more open place where wind could help separate grain from chaff.
But Gideon was working in concealment.
He wasn't looking for a fight.
He was trying to protect his food.
Then the angel of the LORD appeared.
And the greeting was almost shocking.
"The LORD is with thee, thou mighty man of valour." — Judges 6:12, KJV
Can you imagine Gideon's face?
Mighty man of valor?
He was hiding.
He had no army.
No military reputation was mentioned.
No visible evidence that he could deliver an entire nation.
Yet God addressed him in terms of the calling He was about to give him.
In Hebrew, the expression is גִּבּוֹר הֶחָיִל — gibbôr heḥayil, commonly understood in this context as "mighty man of valor" or "mighty warrior."
The words do not mean that Gideon had already become fearless.
They announce a calling that seems completely beyond his present circumstances.
And here is something beautiful.
God wasn't unaware of the winepress.
He knew exactly where Gideon was.
He knew about the Midianites.
He knew about the fear.
He knew about the questions Gideon was carrying.
Yet He called Gideon into a purpose that Gideon could not accomplish by his own strength.
Maybe you need to hear that.
Your present fear does not necessarily define the limits of what God can do through your obedience.
Your past failures do not place you beyond His mercy.
And your hidden struggles are not hidden from Him.
But Gideon's response was not a triumphant declaration of faith.
It was a question.
"If the LORD be with us, why then is all this befallen us?" — Judges 6:13, KJV
There it is.
The question that many Christians have whispered when nobody was listening.
If God is with me, why am I suffering?
If God is faithful, why did everything collapse?
If God hears prayer, why has this burden lasted so long?
Gideon even asked where the wonders were that his ancestors had described.
He knew the stories of deliverance from Egypt.
He knew what God had done before.
But he couldn't reconcile those testimonies with what he was experiencing.
And this is where the passage becomes especially uncomfortable.
Israel's suffering had a spiritual context.

Judges 6:1 tells us that the Israelites had done evil in the sight of the LORD. Earlier in the chapter, a prophet reminded them that God had delivered them from Egypt and commanded them not to fear the gods of the Amorites.
But they had not obeyed His voice.
Israel was not merely experiencing political oppression.
The nation had turned away from the God who had rescued them.
Their circumstances were connected to covenant unfaithfulness.
That matters because the Bible does not invite us to turn Gideon's story into the simplistic claim that every personal hardship is punishment for some hidden sin.
Scripture does not teach that.
But it does require us to confront the reality that God's people can become spiritually compromised while still crying out for His help.
And that is a frightening possibility.
We can want God to remove the consequences while resisting the repentance He calls us to embrace.
We can beg Him to change our circumstances while refusing to surrender the idols occupying our hearts.
We can want rescue without transformation.
But God's mercy is greater than a temporary improvement in our situation.
He calls us back to Himself.
And Gideon's story is about to show us how seriously God takes that relationship.
The LORD commissioned Gideon to deliver Israel from Midian.
Gideon protested.
His clan was weak, and he considered himself the least in his father's house.
He saw his inadequacy.
God answered with His presence.
"Surely I will be with thee." — Judges 6:16, KJV
Notice what God did not say.
He did not tell Gideon that his family background was secretly impressive.
He did not flatter him into confidence.
He did not claim that Gideon already possessed everything necessary for victory.
He promised to be with him.
That is the foundation of biblical courage.
Not confidence that we are enough.
Confidence that God is faithful.
And then Gideon made a request.
He asked for a sign that the One speaking with him truly was the One He claimed to be.
He asked the visitor to remain while he prepared a gift.
And this is where the story takes its astonishing turn.
Judges 6:19 says Gideon went in and prepared a young goat, along with unleavened cakes made from an ephah of flour.
An ephah was a substantial measure, commonly estimated at roughly 20 to 22 liters in capacity, though ancient measures varied.
This was not a tiny snack casually placed before a traveler.
Gideon prepared a considerable provision.
He placed the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot.
Then he brought everything beneath the oak and presented it.
Picture the moment.
The nation is suffering.
Food is precious.
Gideon has been hiding grain from raiders.
Yet now he brings this prepared meal to the mysterious visitor.
The passage does not explicitly tell us everything Gideon understood about the visitor's identity at this point.
But we know he was seeking confirmation from God.
He had asked for a sign.
And he was about to receive one he would never forget.
The angel of God instructed him to place the meat and unleavened cakes upon a rock and pour the broth over them.
Gideon obeyed.
And then it happened.

"Then the angel of the LORD put forth the end of the staff that was in his hand, and touched the flesh and the unleavened cakes; and there rose up fire out of the rock, and consumed the flesh and the unleavened cakes. Then the angel of the LORD departed out of his sight." — Judges 6:21, KJV
Read that again.
Fire came out of the rock.
Not from a torch.
Not from a cooking fire Gideon had prepared.
Not from a human hand striking flint.
The angel touched the food with the end of his staff, and fire rose from the rock itself.
The meat was consumed.
The unleavened cakes were consumed.
And the angel disappeared.
One moment, Gideon was standing before a visitor.
The next, he was standing before the evidence of a supernatural encounter.
The Hebrew description is striking.
וַתַּעַל הָאֵשׁ מִן־הַצּוּר — vattaʿal ha'esh min-hatstsur.
Literally, in natural English: "And the fire went up from the rock."
The Hebrew word אֵשׁ — esh means "fire."
The word צוּר — tsur means "rock" or "rocky mass."
The verb עָלָה — alah carries the sense of ascending, going up, or rising.
The narrative emphasizes the extraordinary source and movement of the fire.
It rose from the rock and consumed what Gideon had placed upon it.
But why?
Why would God use fire?
Why not simply speak from heaven?
Why not give Gideon another verbal assurance?
Why consume the food?
The first answer is found in the immediate context.
The fire was a divine sign confirming that Gideon was not merely speaking to an ordinary traveler.
Gideon had asked for a sign.
God graciously provided one.
The food became the setting for a visible demonstration of divine power.
The narrative resembles other biblical moments when fire consumes an offering in connection with God's revealed presence.
In Leviticus 9:24, fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering.
In 1 Kings 18:38, fire from the LORD consumed Elijah's sacrifice, along with the wood, stones, dust, and water.
In 1 Chronicles 21:26, the LORD answered David by fire from heaven upon the altar.
These passages are not identical.
Their historical settings and purposes differ.
But they share an important biblical pattern.
Fire can serve as a visible manifestation of God's holy power and His response to an offering.
In Gideon's case, the text does not explicitly call the prepared food a formal burnt offering or explain that its consumption constituted atonement for sin.
We should not force those claims into the passage.
What Scripture does show is that God answered Gideon's request with a miraculous sign involving fire and the food he presented.
The rock became the location of the sign.
The staff was the instrument used by the angel.
And the consuming fire confirmed that something far greater than an ordinary meal had taken place.
But the story does not end with Gideon celebrating.
That is what makes the next moment so powerful.
The fire had disappeared.
The angel was gone.
And Gideon suddenly realized the seriousness of what had happened.
He cried out:
"Alas, O Lord GOD! for because I have seen an angel of the LORD face to face." — Judges 6:22, KJV
He was terrified.
Why?
Because Gideon understood that he had encountered a messenger associated with the holy presence of God.
Throughout the Old Testament, encounters with divine holiness could produce profound fear.
Human beings were not dealing with a manageable religious experience.
They were confronting the reality of the living God.
And in Judges 6, the language moves between the angel of the LORD speaking and the LORD Himself addressing Gideon.
This has led Christians throughout history to discuss whether the angel of the LORD in passages like this represents a manifestation of the preincarnate Christ.
Some Christian interpreters understand these appearances as Christophanies.
Others emphasize the biblical pattern in which a divine messenger speaks with God's authority and represents His presence.
The passage itself does not explicitly identify the angel as Jesus Christ.
We can acknowledge the theological discussion without claiming more certainty than the text provides.
What is unmistakable is Gideon's reaction.
He believed he was in mortal danger.
He had asked for confirmation.
He received fire.
And now he feared that encountering the holy presence of God would cost him his life.
Have you ever experienced a moment when the truth about God suddenly became more personal than you were prepared for?
Perhaps you heard a sermon about forgiveness and realized how much bitterness you were carrying.
Perhaps you opened Scripture and encountered a command you had been avoiding.
Perhaps you were confronted by the seriousness of sin you had spent years excusing.
At first, you thought you were simply looking for encouragement.
Then the Word of God exposed something deeper.
Something painful.
Something you could no longer pretend wasn't there.
The problem was not that God had become cruel.
The problem was that His holiness was revealing what you had learned to hide.
And that is where some people run away.
They assume conviction means God wants nothing to do with them.
They confuse exposure with abandonment.
They think the moment their sin is brought into the light, their hope is gone.
But watch what happens to Gideon.
Because the most beautiful words in this entire account are not spoken before the fire.
They come after it.
The LORD says:
"Peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die." — Judges 6:23, KJV
Can you feel the contrast?
Gideon expected death.
God spoke peace.
Gideon was overwhelmed by fear.
God told him not to be afraid.
Gideon thought the encounter might destroy him.
God assured him that he would live.
The Hebrew opening is simple and deeply meaningful.
שָׁלוֹם לְךָ — shalom lekha.
"Peace to you."
The word שָׁלוֹם — shalom can communicate peace, well-being, wholeness, and welfare, depending on its context.
Here it is a direct word of reassurance to a frightened man.
God was not telling Gideon that the Midianites had already disappeared.
The oppression was not yet over.
The battle had not yet been fought.
Gideon had not yet gathered his army.
His circumstances were still dangerous.
Yet God spoke peace to him in the middle of that unfinished story.
The peace came before the victory.
That deserves to stay with you.
Because many of us have been waiting for every problem to disappear before we allow ourselves to rest in God's faithfulness.
We say we'll have peace when the debt is paid.
When the medical report changes.
When the relationship is restored.
When the temptation finally loses its grip.
When the family stops fighting.
When the anxiety disappears.
When our lives look the way we thought they would.
But Gideon was given peace before the battle.
Not because the battle was imaginary.
Not because suffering didn't matter.
But because the God who called him had not abandoned him.
And that points us toward something even greater.
Gideon built an altar and called it:
יְהוָה שָׁלוֹם — YHWH Shalom.
"The LORD is Peace."
Judges 6:24 records the name and says the altar remained in Ophrah at the time the account was written.
Think about the location.
An altar declaring the LORD's peace stood in a land still suffering under Midianite oppression.
That altar was a testimony that peace with God was not dependent upon Gideon first achieving military success.
It was grounded in God's gracious word.
And this is where we must move carefully from Gideon's story to the Gospel of Jesus Christ.
Because if we read this account merely as a motivational story about becoming brave, we miss something far more important.
Gideon needed deliverance.
Israel needed restoration.
But humanity's deepest problem is greater than fear, poverty, or oppression.
Our deepest problem is sin.
We have turned away from the God who made us.
We have loved created things more than the Creator.
We have defended our pride, justified our selfishness, and resisted the authority of the One who gives us life.
Some sins are public scandals.
Others remain carefully hidden.
Some destroy reputations overnight.
Others slowly corrupt the heart while everything on the outside still looks respectable.
And Scripture does not allow us to pretend that religious activity can erase our guilt.
Romans 3:23 says:
"For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God."
All.
The openly rebellious.
The secretly addicted.
The bitter.
The proud.
The person whose marriage collapsed because of betrayal.
The churchgoer who knows all the worship songs but has been living a double life.
The person who smiles during Sunday service while privately drowning in shame.
And yes, even the person writing these words needs the mercy of Christ.
Nobody stands before God on the strength of a flawless record.
Nobody earns reconciliation with God by appearing more respectable than the next person.
We need grace.
And the Gospel announces that God has provided what we could never provide for ourselves.
Jesus Christ, the eternal Son of God, took on human flesh.
He lived without sin.
He willingly gave Himself on the cross.
He bore the judgment that sinners deserve.
He rose bodily from the dead.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith receives forgiveness and reconciliation with God.
This is not merely a message about feeling better.
It is the announcement of what God has accomplished through His Son.
Romans 5:1 declares:
"Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ."
There is that word again.
Peace.
But now the New Testament reveals the saving work through which sinners are brought into peace with God.
Gideon's altar was called "The LORD is Peace."
Jesus Christ is the One through whom we receive peace with God.
The connection is not that the rock in Judges 6 is explicitly identified as Christ, or that the fire directly symbolizes the crucifixion.
The passage does not say those things.
The deeper connection is found in the unfolding revelation of God's redemptive character.
The God who graciously reassured a trembling Gideon is the God who, in the fullness of time, sent His Son to reconcile sinners to Himself.
And through Christ, the peace we need is not merely relief from external danger.
It is reconciliation with the holy God against whom we have sinned.
Colossians 1:20 speaks of God making peace through the blood of Christ's cross.
That is the center of our hope.
Not the strength of our offering.
Not the intensity of our emotions.
Not our ability to maintain a perfect spiritual performance.
Jesus.
His righteousness.
His sacrifice.
His resurrection.
His mercy.
And this is why the fire from Gideon's rock should not become a formula for demanding supernatural signs whenever we feel uncertain.
The Bible does not command Christians to repeat Gideon's experience.
It does not promise that fire will rise from stones when we offer something to God.
And it does not teach that the size of a financial gift determines whether God will accept us.
Gideon's experience was a particular event in the history of God's dealings with Israel.
Its lasting significance is not a technique to reproduce.
It is a revelation of God's power, holiness, patience, and gracious reassurance.
And it challenges us with a question that reaches far beyond ancient Ophrah.
What do you do when God confronts the fear, unbelief, or disobedience you've been hiding?
Do you run?
Do you make excuses?
Do you blame your past?
Do you convince yourself that you are too damaged to change?
Or do you listen when His Word calls you to repentance and faith?
Because there is a difference between being exposed and being condemned.
The Holy Spirit's work of conviction directs sinners toward the truth about Christ.
The Gospel does not minimize sin.
It reveals a Savior sufficient to forgive it.
And when a sinner comes to Jesus in genuine repentance and faith, the answer is not, "Make yourself worthy first."
The answer is grace.
Not cheap grace that gives permission to continue loving sin.
Saving grace that forgives, renews, and teaches us to turn away from ungodliness.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's grace trains believers to renounce ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace does not leave us comfortably chained to the very things Christ came to save us from.
It changes us.
Sometimes slowly.
Sometimes painfully.
Often through repentance that must be practiced again and again as we grow in holiness.
But always with Christ as our hope.
And perhaps that is the part of Gideon's story you needed most.
He was not instantly transformed into a man who never struggled again.
Read the chapters that follow.
He still needed reassurance.
He still wrestled with fear.
God continued dealing patiently with him.
And later, Gideon's own story contains sobering evidence that even a person greatly used by God can make serious mistakes.
The Bible does not present him as a flawless hero.
That is important.
Because if your faith depends on imagining that God's servants never struggle, every honest look at yourself will leave you discouraged.
But if your hope rests in the faithfulness of God, you can face your weakness truthfully.
You can confess sin without pretending it is harmless.
You can repent without believing that your failure is greater than Christ's mercy.
You can seek help without maintaining a religious image.
You can obey even while your hands are trembling.
And you can remember that the Savior who calls His people to holiness is also the Savior who intercedes for them.
Maybe you're reading this while carrying something nobody knows about.
A secret habit.
A broken promise.
An old betrayal.
A season of spiritual coldness.
A prayer life that has become almost silent.
Or perhaps you are not hiding sin so much as hiding pain.
You've been wounded.
Exhausted.
Disappointed.
You have watched other people testify about answered prayers while wondering why your own story feels unfinished.
And somewhere along the way, you started confusing your difficult circumstances with God's absence.
Remember Gideon.
The Midianites were still there when God said, "Peace."
The threat had not vanished.
The deliverance was still ahead.
But God had spoken.
That does not mean every painful situation will resolve the way we want.
It does not mean faithful Christians are promised freedom from every illness, financial struggle, or earthly tragedy.
Jesus Himself told His disciples that they would experience tribulation in this world.
But He also told them to take courage because He had overcome the world.
Christian peace is not a guarantee that tomorrow will be easy.
It is the assurance that through Christ, our relationship with God rests on His saving grace rather than the instability of our circumstances.
And that changes how we endure.
It changes how we repent.
It changes how we suffer.
It changes how we rise after failure.
Because the Gospel does not say your past never happened.
It says that your past does not have to be the final word over a life surrendered to Jesus Christ.
The scandal may be real.
The consequences may still need to be faced.
The people you hurt may need time to heal.
Trust may need to be rebuilt.
Confession may require courage.
Repentance may demand costly changes.
Grace does not erase responsibility.
But through Jesus Christ, grace opens the door to forgiveness, restoration, and a transformed life.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because the Savior is sufficient.
Not because our wounds are imaginary.
But because Christ is able to meet us in the truth.
Not because we can rewrite our history by pretending.
But because Jesus can redeem a life that seemed beyond hope.
And now I want to ask you something personal.
When you think about Gideon standing before that rock, watching the fire consume his offering, which part of the story feels most like your life right now?
Is it the hiding?
The questions?
The fear of being exposed?
The struggle to believe that God can use someone as weak as you?
Or is it the desperate need to hear those words again?
"Peace be unto thee; fear not."
You do not need to pretend in order to answer.
You do not have to disclose private details or expose someone else's story.
Sometimes a few honest words can remind another struggling believer that they are not alone.
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else needs to seek Christ rather than surrender to despair.
And please don't keep this message only to yourself.
Think about the person who has quietly disappeared from fellowship.
The friend who used to speak passionately about Jesus but now seems spiritually exhausted.
The family member who believes their mistakes have placed them beyond forgiveness.
The believer who is smiling publicly but struggling privately.
Not merely to increase its reach, but because Scripture-centered encouragement may reach someone you cannot reach through a private conversation.

We want this community to be a place where biblical truth is not watered down, where repentance is taken seriously, where wounded people are treated with compassion, and where Jesus Christ remains the center of every message.
Not a platform built around personalities.
Not a place where emotional excitement replaces sound doctrine.
But a growing community committed to Scripture, discipleship, prayer, encouragement, and the transforming Gospel of Jesus Christ.
And if these messages have been strengthening your walk with God, I want to invite you to consider something more.
Not because God requires you to support this particular ministry.
And certainly not because your salvation, forgiveness, or spiritual blessing can be purchased.
The Gospel is freely given through Jesus Christ.
But those who have been encouraged by a ministry may freely choose to help sustain and expand its work.
Throughout the New Testament, believers supported Gospel ministry through willing, generous giving.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Philippians 4:15–17 also shows how believers participated in Paul's ministry through material support.
It may be part of your personal giving, alongside your responsibilities to your local church, family, and others in need.
It should never be presented as a mandatory tithe owed to Gospel Warrior or as a replacement for faithful participation in your local church.
But it can be a meaningful way to participate in spreading biblical teaching.
Think about the believer who is one message away from opening their Bible again.
The exhausted parent who reads a devotional after everyone else has gone to sleep.
The young person struggling with temptation.
The man carrying shame over a decision he deeply regrets.
The woman who has been quietly praying for strength to begin again.
We cannot know how God may use a particular article.
But we can faithfully make biblical resources available and trust Him with the results.
That is the heart behind this invitation.
And there is already more available than many people realize.
These free resources are part of our desire to make spiritual nourishment more accessible.
The library is not a replacement for Scripture, the local church, or personal discipleship.
It is an additional resource to help you study, reflect, and grow in the truth of God's Word.
It is Jesus Christ Himself.
You are no less welcome.
You are no less valued.
And your ability to give money has nothing to do with the worth of your soul before God.
You can still pray for this ministry.
You can still help the Gospel reach people through the simple act of sharing truth with love.
Our mission is to proclaim the Gospel faithfully, nurture disciples, and point people toward the Lord Jesus Christ.
And that brings us back to Gideon.
Back to the winepress.
Back to the frightened man who did not see himself as a mighty warrior.
Back to the meal.
Back to the rock.
Back to the fire.
Gideon came seeking confirmation.
He witnessed a sign of divine power.
He trembled before God's holiness.
And he heard the words that changed the meaning of that moment.
"Peace be unto thee; fear not: thou shalt not die."
What began with fear ended with an altar bearing the name of the LORD's peace.
And although Gideon's life was far from perfect, that encounter became part of the story of how God delivered Israel.
Perhaps you are still in your own winepress.
Perhaps you are hiding from the judgment of others.
Perhaps you are struggling with questions you have been afraid to say out loud.
Perhaps your circumstances have not changed, and the battle ahead still looks impossible.
But you do not need to manufacture a supernatural sign to find hope.
God has already given us His Word.
And the clearest revelation of His saving love is Jesus Christ, crucified and risen.
Come to Him.
Not with excuses.
Not with a carefully edited version of your life.
Not with the illusion that you can make yourself righteous.
Come with repentance.
Come with faith.
Come trusting the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
And if you belong to Him but have wandered, stop running from the truth.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
Seek reconciliation where it is possible and appropriate.
Return to prayer.
Return to Scripture.
Return to the fellowship and accountability of God's people.
Keep your eyes on Jesus.
Because the most important question is not whether God will make fire rise from a rock in your lifetime.
The question is whether you will trust the Savior whom God has already revealed.
And maybe that is what makes Gideon's story so unforgettable.
The fire was astonishing.
The disappearing messenger was terrifying.
The divine calling was overwhelming.
But the words that followed were tender.
"Peace be unto thee."
A frightened man heard those words in a troubled nation.
And centuries later, through the finished work of Jesus Christ, repentant sinners can know the peace of reconciliation with God.
So before you leave this article, take a moment.
Not to chase an emotional experience.
Not to make a promise you have no intention of keeping.
But to examine your heart before the Lord.
What have you been hiding?
What truth have you been resisting?
Where have you allowed fear to become louder than God's Word?
And what would obedience look like today?
Maybe it begins with a confession.
Maybe with an apology.
Maybe with asking someone to pray with you.
Maybe with opening your Bible after months of neglect.
Maybe with surrendering a sin you have spent years defending.
Or maybe with simply praying:

"Lord Jesus, I need Your mercy. Forgive my sins. Teach me to trust You. Help me turn away from what dishonors You and walk in the truth of Your Word. My hope is not in my strength, but in Your finished work. Amen."
If that prayer reflects the desire of your heart, don't let the moment end as another passing feeling.
Seek Christ in His Word.
Find a faithful, Bible-teaching church.
Walk with believers who will encourage you, pray with you, and help you grow in obedience.
And remember this.
The Christian life is not sustained by one emotional moment.
It is a life of faith in the risen Savior.
But above every invitation, hear this one:
Come to Jesus Christ.
He is greater than your fear.
His grace is sufficient for every sinner who comes to Him in repentance and faith.
And His resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final victory.
The fire from the rock consumed Gideon's food.
But the greater wonder was the mercy of God toward a trembling man.
And through Jesus Christ, we are invited to behold an even greater mercy.
The man who feared he would die in God's presence heard the words of peace; the sinner who trusts in the crucified and risen Christ finds peace with God Himself.
